title: The pilgrimages
hook: tradition says he traveled with Sikhs to pilgrim sites and spoke against the pilgrim tax

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manjis: plain seats where teachers, women and men, held the sangat near home. Your line was spread it far. Who did you tell, and what did they ask? Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

Pay here before you pray. A gate at the edge of a holy river, and someone collecting a fee from every traveler who wants to bathe. A family has walked for days. They're tired, they've saved for this, and now there's a charge just to reach the water. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Amar Das traveling with his Sikhs to pilgrim places, the crowded river towns where people came to bathe and remember God. And it remembers him speaking up about a tax laid on the pilgrims themselves.
screen: `PAY HERE BEFORE YOU PRAY.` → `A FAMILY AT THE RIVER GATE.` → `THE GURU AMONG THE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: Start with why a Guru goes to a pilgrim town at all. The Sikh Gurus taught that the true pilgrimage is inward. Guru Nanak puts it plainly in the Japji, paraphrased: I would bathe at the place of pilgrimage if that pleased Him; without pleasing Him, what good is the bathing? The Sikh word for a pilgrim place is tirath, and the Japji itself speaks of bathing at a tirath within. So when tradition shows Guru Amar Das going to those crowded places, Sikh tellings present it this way: he went where the people already were. Seekers gathered there, hungry for God, and the Guru met them in the crowd, sang the Word, and fed people. Not to mock their journey, but to share what the Gurus had found. Then the tax. Tradition says the Guru spoke against a charge laid on pilgrims, and some accounts say the emperor Akbar later lifted it. Whatever the details, the instinct is clear, and it runs through the stories of his time. No one should have to pay to come near God. Tradition says the well at Goindval was open to every caste. The langar row asks no fee. The Guru's Word is sung for anyone who walks in. A tax on pilgrims put a price on the very thing the Gurus kept giving away. So today's line has two sides. Free the pilgrims from unfair charges. And remember that the pilgrimage inward doesn't need a gate at all.
screen: `TIRATH: THE PLACE OF PILGRIMAGE.` · `HE WENT WHERE THE PEOPLE WERE.` · `NO PRICE TO COME NEAR GOD.` · `THE PILGRIMAGE WITHOUT A GATE.` · then, large: `FREE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: question one unfair charge. Settle, and let the breath slow. Bring to mind a cost someone has to pay just to belong, to worship, to learn or to be helped. A fee, a form, a rule, a look at the door. It might be in your workplace, your town or your own house. Hold it without anger for a moment. Ask simply: who is this keeping out, and does it need to? Then let the breath carry you to the tirath within that the Japji speaks of. If you pray, you can say Waheguru there. The bell holds the time.
The pilgrimages. Guru Amar Das, tradition says, went among the pilgrims, shared the Word, and spoke against a tax that charged them to come near God. Today's word.
Your line: free pilgrims. Today, ask one polite question about the unfair charge you found, or quietly cover a cost so someone else can come in. Day one thousand one hundred eighty-nine.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Amar Das's journeys and the pilgrim tax in histories and katha, and they speak of an inward pilgrimage; gurdwaras are open to visitors without any fee.

fork.setup: pilgrims must pay a tax to reach the holy water. you're the Guru, traveling among them. what do you do?
options: say nothing; it's not your concern.
tell the pilgrims to stop going.
fork.reveal: tradition says he spoke against it. no one, in the Gurus' teaching, should have to pay to come near God.

original.note: a place of pilgrimage; the Japji also speaks of a tirath within.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs simply don't go on pilgrimage.
what it means: the Gurus taught an inward pilgrimage, and still went where pilgrims gathered.
what a scholar hears: Japji 6: 'tirath nava je tis bhava': I'd bathe at the tirath if it pleased Him.
